videos.script: Lesson 4 wrote a program that printed one fixed sentence. Real programs keep values, change them and pass them around, and for that they need names. {{forms}} Go has two ways to declare a variable. The long one starts with the word var. It works everywhere, and it lets you say the type out loud. {{short}} The short one is colon equals. It works only inside a function, and it works the type out from the value. Most of the Go you will read uses it. {{errors}} The compiler is strict about both. Declare a variable and never use it, and the program does not build. Use colon equals where nothing is new, and it refuses that too. You will see each message exactly as the compiler prints it. {{const}} Then constants. A constant is fixed when the program is compiled. It can hold a number far larger than any variable, right up to the moment it has to fit in one. {{close}} By the end you will know which form to reach for, and what each refusal means.
